title: GOD STRUCK AN ENTIRE NATION BECAUSE ONE MAN REFUSED TO BOW—BUT THE REAL STORY OF EGYPT'S TEN PLAGUES IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK
paragraphs: GOD STRUCK AN ENTIRE NATION BECAUSE ONE MAN REFUSED TO BOW—BUT THE REAL STORY OF EGYPT'S TEN PLAGUES IS MORE TERRIFYING THAN YOU THINK

Why did Egyptian families suffer because Pharaoh hardened his heart? Was God punishing innocent people for one ruler's rebellion? And what does the blood on an ancient doorway reveal about the mercy of Jesus Christ? The answer in Exodus 7–12 may change how you understand judgment, suffering, repentance, and grace forever.
Imagine waking up tomorrow morning and discovering that the water coming from your faucet looks like blood.
Not a little discoloration.
Blood.
The rivers are red. The fish are dying. The smell of death is rising from the water. Your children are thirsty, and you cannot give them anything to drink.
You have done nothing to provoke this disaster.
You are not the king.
You did not issue the orders.
You are an ordinary person trying to survive another day.
And somewhere inside a palace, the most powerful man in your country is refusing to listen to God.
Then the frogs come.
Then the insects.
Then disease.
Then darkness.
And finally, something so devastating that an entire nation wakes up screaming.
Now imagine being an Egyptian mother, holding your firstborn child as the sun disappears beyond the horizon, unaware that the darkest night in your nation's history is approaching.
What would you ask God?
Perhaps the same question that has troubled believers for centuries.
Why did God strike an entire nation because of Pharaoh's actions?
Was it justice?
Was it collective punishment?
Was God demonstrating His power without regard for the suffering of ordinary people?
Or is there something happening beneath the surface of Exodus that we miss when we read the story too quickly?
Because the ten plagues were not simply ten disasters.
They were a confrontation between the Creator and an empire that had turned human beings into property.
They were an exposure of the cruelty hidden beneath Egypt's magnificent civilization.
They were a warning that political power does not make anyone greater than God.
And astonishingly, even within the judgment, there were repeated opportunities for mercy.
But to understand why the plagues happened, we must first remember something the story never allows us to forget.
Before Egypt cried over its firstborn sons, Israel had already cried over its murdered children.
And God had heard every cry.
Long before Moses stood before Pharaoh, the Israelites were living under brutal oppression.
They were not guests enjoying Egypt's hospitality anymore.
They were slaves.
Their bodies belonged to their masters. Their labor built the wealth of an empire. Their suffering was treated as the necessary price of Egyptian prosperity.
Exodus 1 describes the Egyptians making the Israelites' lives bitter through forced labor.
But Pharaoh's cruelty went further.
He commanded that Hebrew baby boys be killed.
Think about that.
Before the Nile became blood, Pharaoh had ordered innocent blood to be shed.
Before Egyptian families experienced grief, Hebrew mothers had already been forced to confront the possibility of losing their sons.
The empire had normalized suffering as long as the victims were Israelites.
And this is where the moral foundation of the story begins.
God was not attacking a peaceful society because its ruler made one unfortunate decision.
He was confronting an oppressive system that had been destroying lives for generations.
Exodus 2:23–25 tells us that the Israelites groaned under their slavery and cried out, and God heard them.
The Hebrew verb translated as "heard" is שָׁמַע (shamaʿ).
It means to hear or listen, and in this context it emphasizes that the suffering of God's covenant people had not escaped His attention.
He was not absent.
He was not indifferent.
He had not forgotten His promises to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that right now.
You have been praying for something that seems to remain unchanged.
You have watched someone misuse authority while others suffer the consequences.
You have wondered why God appears silent when evil seems so loud.
But silence is not the same as indifference.
The God who heard Israel's groaning is not deaf to suffering.
And when He finally confronted Pharaoh, He did not begin with the death of Egypt's firstborn.
He began with a command.
"Let my people go."
That command was repeated throughout the confrontation.
In Exodus 7:16, Moses delivers God's message that Pharaoh must release Israel so they can serve the Lord.
The Hebrew expression שַׁלַּח אֶת־עַמִּי (shallach et-ʿammi) means "Send away my people" or, naturally in English, "Let my people go."
Notice something remarkable.
God was not asking Pharaoh to improve the Israelites' working conditions.
He was not asking for shorter shifts, better food, or more humane treatment.
He was demanding their release.
Because the Israelites were never Pharaoh's property.
They belonged to God.
And that is the first truth Pharaoh refused to accept.
He believed that because he possessed political authority, he possessed ultimate authority.
He could command armies.
He could control labor.
He could determine who lived under his rule and who suffered beneath it.
But he could not command the Creator of heaven and earth.
In Exodus 5:2, Pharaoh had already revealed the arrogance at the center of the conflict:
"Who is the LORD, that I should obey his voice to let Israel go?" (KJV)
That question would become the haunting backdrop of the plagues.
Who is the LORD?
The Nile would answer.
The land would answer.
The heavens would answer.
And eventually, the palace itself would be forced to confront the answer.
But here is where the story becomes uncomfortable.
Pharaoh was not the only person who suffered from Pharaoh's pride.
Ordinary Egyptians suffered too.
And Scripture does not pretend otherwise.
When the Nile turned to blood, the fish died and the river became foul. The Egyptians could not drink its water, and people dug near the river searching for water.
When frogs overwhelmed the land, they entered houses, bedrooms, and places where food was prepared.
When insects swarmed, life became unbearable.
When disease struck livestock, Egypt's economy and food supply were threatened.
When hail fell, it destroyed crops, trees, and exposed people and animals.
When locusts arrived, they consumed what remained.
When darkness covered Egypt, ordinary life stopped.
And when the final plague came, grief reached into Egyptian households.
The text gives us no permission to dismiss their suffering as insignificant.
These were human beings.
Parents.
Children.
Workers.
Families.
People made in the image of God, even though they lived within a nation that had oppressed His people.
So why did they suffer?
Because Pharaoh's evil was not merely a private spiritual problem.
It was embedded in a national system.
Egypt's prosperity depended, in part, on Israel's enslavement. Pharaoh's commands were enforced through institutions, officials, and a society structured around royal power.
That does not mean every Egyptian was equally guilty.
The Bible does not say that every Egyptian personally supported Pharaoh's cruelty or deserved identical judgment.
But it does reveal a sobering reality.
When evil becomes institutionalized, its consequences rarely remain confined to the people who initiated it.
A ruler's pride can become a nation's catastrophe.
A leader's stubbornness can endanger people who never chose the conflict.
And a society can suffer terribly when those holding power refuse correction.
We still recognize that reality.
A father can make destructive decisions that wound his children.
A corrupt leader can devastate communities.
An abusive authority figure can create suffering far beyond the original act of wrongdoing.
Sin is never as isolated as we want to believe.
Its consequences spread.
And yet Exodus reveals something more complex than the idea that every Egyptian suffered because of one man's decisions.
The plagues were also God's judgment against Egypt's oppression and its false claims to divine power.
In Exodus 12:12, God declares that He will execute judgment against the gods of Egypt.
The Hebrew word שְׁפָטִים (shefatim) means "judgments."
This is important.
The plagues were not random explosions of anger.
They were acts of divine judgment, revealing the Lord's authority over the natural world and exposing the helplessness of Egypt's religious and political powers.
The Nile, upon which Egyptian life depended, could not protect itself.
Egypt's magicians could imitate certain signs but could not reverse God's judgments.
The land, animals, weather, and light were all shown to be under the authority of the Creator.
Some interpreters connect individual plagues with particular Egyptian deities, but Scripture does not provide a definitive one-to-one identification for every plague.
The central biblical point is greater than any speculative list.
No god worshiped by Egypt could stand against the LORD.
And the purpose was not merely destruction.
God repeatedly declared that these events would reveal who He is.
Exodus 7:5 says the Egyptians would know that He is the LORD.
In Exodus 9:16, God tells Pharaoh that His power is being displayed so that His name may be proclaimed throughout the earth.
This was a public confrontation with a public purpose.
The Lord was revealing Himself as the God who judges oppression, keeps His covenant, and rules over creation.
But then we encounter one of the most difficult questions in the entire narrative.
If Pharaoh was responsible for resisting God, why does Exodus repeatedly say that God hardened Pharaoh's heart?
Did God make Pharaoh stubborn and then punish him for being stubborn?
Was Pharaoh ever given a genuine opportunity to repent?
This question deserves more than a convenient religious slogan.
The Hebrew word often translated as "hardened" is חָזַק (chazaq), which can mean to be strong, become firm, or strengthen.
Another important Hebrew verb is כָּבֵד (kaved), which carries the sense of being heavy or weighty and, when applied to the heart, can describe stubbornness or unresponsiveness.
The narrative uses several expressions to describe Pharaoh's resistance.
Sometimes Pharaoh hardens his own heart.
Sometimes the text describes his heart becoming hard.
And sometimes God is explicitly said to harden it.
Exodus 8:15, for example, describes Pharaoh hardening his heart after experiencing relief.
Exodus 9:34 says Pharaoh and his servants hardened their hearts after the hail stopped.
Exodus 9:12 explicitly says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart.
We must not erase either side of the account.
God's sovereign purpose is real.
Pharaoh's moral responsibility is also real.
The text does not offer a complete philosophical explanation of how divine sovereignty and human responsibility operate together.
Christians have understood this relationship in different ways.

Some emphasize God's judicial hardening of a ruler already committed to rebellion. Others place greater emphasis on God's sovereign determination to accomplish His redemptive purpose through Pharaoh's resistance.
But the narrative itself makes one thing unmistakable.
Pharaoh was not portrayed as a humble man begging to obey God while God cruelly prevented him.
He was already an oppressor.
He had already refused God's command.
He repeatedly responded to relief by returning to resistance.
And his stubbornness was not harmless.
People were suffering because he would not release those he had no right to enslave.
There is something frighteningly familiar about that.
Have you ever promised God you would change if He would just get you through one more crisis?
You prayed when the fear was unbearable.
You cried when everything seemed to be collapsing.
You promised to forgive.
You promised to repent.
You promised to stop hiding.
Then the pressure lifted.
Life became comfortable again.
And slowly, you returned to the very thing you had begged God to deliver you from.
Pharaoh repeatedly experienced that pattern.
The frogs were removed.
The hail stopped.
The immediate suffering eased.
And his resistance returned.
Sometimes the most dangerous moment in a person's spiritual life is not when the trouble begins, but when the trouble ends and repentance is forgotten.
That is why this ancient story reaches beyond Egypt.
Pharaoh's heart forces us to examine our own.
Not because every stubborn decision brings a plague.
Not because every hardship is punishment for a hidden sin.
Jesus explicitly rejected the assumption that every sufferer is more sinful than others (Luke 13:1–5; John 9:1–3).
But because human beings are remarkably capable of recognizing God's mercy without surrendering to God's authority.
We want relief without repentance.
Forgiveness without confession.
Deliverance without obedience.
We want God to remove the consequences while we continue protecting the thing that caused the damage.
And that is not freedom.
That is bondage wearing a different face.
Yet even in Egypt, the Lord's judgments were accompanied by warnings.
Before the devastating hail, God instructed that people and livestock be brought into shelter.
Exodus 9:20–21 records a striking distinction.
Some of Pharaoh's servants feared the word of the LORD and brought their servants and livestock indoors.
Others disregarded the warning and left them in the field.
Read that again.
Some Egyptians listened to God and acted to protect their households.
The narrative does not portray every Egyptian as spiritually identical.
Even within a nation under judgment, individuals responded differently to God's word.
And their responses mattered.
That detail changes the way we understand the plagues.
God's warnings were not meaningless theater.
They provided opportunities for people to recognize His authority and respond.
Exodus also distinguishes between Egypt and the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived, during several plagues.
That distinction reveals God's covenant purpose in delivering His people.
But it does not mean the Israelites were morally superior in every respect.
Their rescue was grounded in God's covenant faithfulness and mercy, not in a claim that Israel had never sinned.
And this becomes especially clear when we reach the tenth plague.
The final judgment.
The death of the firstborn.
This is the moment many readers would rather avoid.
Because it is devastating.
Exodus 12:29–30 describes the death of Egypt's firstborn, from Pharaoh's household to the households of those held in captivity.
A great cry rose throughout Egypt.
The Bible does not soften the grief.
And neither should we.
These deaths are not a minor detail inserted to make the story more dramatic.
They confront us with the seriousness of divine judgment and the terrible human cost of the conflict.
We must also remember that God had already called Israel His firstborn son.
In Exodus 4:22–23, the Lord tells Pharaoh that Israel is His firstborn and warns that Pharaoh's refusal to release His son will bring judgment upon Egypt's firstborn.
The final plague was therefore not an unexpected escalation without warning.
It had been announced before the sequence of plagues began.
And the earlier command to kill Hebrew sons gives the judgment an especially sobering moral context.
Still, recognizing that context does not make the grief of Egyptian families emotionally easy.
The Bible does not answer every question we may have about each individual who died.
It does not tell us the eternal destiny of every Egyptian firstborn.
It does not invite us to celebrate the suffering of children.
Instead, it reveals the terrifying seriousness of judgment while moving us toward the astonishing provision of mercy.
Because on that final night, another question was being answered.
How could anyone be protected when judgment passed through the land?
Not by wealth.
Not by social status.
Not by political influence.
Not by claiming to be better than the Egyptians.
God instructed the Israelite households to sacrifice a lamb and place its blood on the doorposts and lintel of their homes.
Exodus 12:13 records God's promise:
"When I see the blood, I will pass over you." (KJV)
The Hebrew word פֶּסַח (pesach) is associated with Passover, and the related verb in Exodus 12:13 describes the Lord passing over or sparing the marked households.
There is a depth here that should stop us in our tracks.
The Israelites were not told to write a record of their good deeds above the doorway.
They were not told to display their family achievements.
They were not told to prove they had lived perfect lives.
They were commanded to respond in faith and obedience to God's provision.
The blood marked the household according to the covenant instructions God had given.
It was not magic.
It was not a human attempt to manipulate heaven.
It was God's appointed sign of protection.
And here, thousands of years later, Christians recognize a profound connection to Jesus Christ.
Not because Exodus 12 directly names Jesus of Nazareth.
It does not.
But because the New Testament explicitly identifies Christ with the Passover sacrifice.
The apostle Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 5:7:
And John the Baptist declares in John 1:29:
"Behold the Lamb of God, which taketh away the sin of the world." (KJV)
Do you see the movement of the biblical story?
In Egypt, the blood of the Passover lamb marked the households God had promised to spare from a particular judgment.
At Calvary, Jesus Christ, the sinless Son of God, offered Himself for sinners.
The Passover and the cross are not identical events, but the New Testament teaches us to see the Passover as part of the redemptive story fulfilled in Christ.
The lamb in Egypt points forward to the greater Lamb.
The deliverance from slavery anticipates the greater deliverance from sin and death.
And the God who rescued His people from Pharaoh is the God who has acted in Jesus Christ to rescue sinners through grace.
This is where the story becomes intensely personal.
Because the deepest question is no longer simply why Pharaoh refused to release Israel.
It becomes:
What is holding your heart captive today?
Maybe it is pride.
You know you need to apologize, but you would rather lose the relationship than admit you were wrong.
Maybe it is bitterness.
Someone wounded you deeply, and although you speak about forgiveness, you keep returning to the memory because resentment has become familiar.
Maybe it is secret sin.
The kind nobody sees when you are sitting in church.
The kind hidden behind worship songs, Bible verses, and carefully chosen photographs.
Maybe it is fear.
You know Christ is calling you to trust Him, but you are terrified of what surrender might cost.
Or perhaps you are not resisting God at all in the way Pharaoh did.
Perhaps you are the one who has been crushed beneath someone else's choices.
You are the exhausted mother.
The betrayed spouse.
The wounded child who grew older without ever receiving an apology.
The faithful believer who keeps asking why the wicked seem to prosper.
Then hear what Exodus says to the oppressed.
God sees. God hears. And evil does not possess unlimited authority over His creation.
But hear what the Gospel says to every sinner, including those who have caused harm.
Repentance is possible.
Forgiveness is available through Jesus Christ.
And no one needs to pretend that their past is clean before coming to the Savior.
The Greek word μετάνοια (metanoia), commonly translated "repentance," speaks of a change of mind or turning, understood in the New Testament as a response to God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Repentance is not merely feeling guilty because something went wrong.
It is turning toward God in recognition of the truth.
It is abandoning the illusion that we can save ourselves.
It is bringing our sins into the light and trusting the mercy of Jesus Christ.
And the Greek word χάρις (charis), translated "grace," reminds us that salvation is God's gift, not something we can purchase or earn.
Ephesians 2:8–9 says:
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: Not of works, lest any man should boast." (KJV)
That truth matters enormously.
Because the Gospel is not the message that good people earn protection while bad people suffer.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose again, and that salvation is offered through Him.
At the cross, we encounter both the seriousness of sin and the immeasurable mercy of God.
Jesus did not come merely to make our lives more comfortable.
He came to save.
He did not excuse sin.
He bore its cost.
He did not tell broken people to repair themselves before approaching Him.
He called them to repent and believe.
And through His death and resurrection, He opened the way to reconciliation with God.
The story that began with a tyrant refusing to release slaves leads us toward the Savior who declares in John 8:36:
"If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed." (KJV)
That is the freedom Pharaoh could never give.
That is the freedom Egypt's wealth could never purchase.
That is the freedom religious performance can never manufacture.
Freedom from sin's condemnation through Christ.
Freedom to belong to God.
Freedom to begin walking in obedience, even while the work of spiritual growth continues.
And perhaps this is the most unexpected lesson of the plagues.
God's judgment is not proof that He has forgotten mercy.
But neither is His mercy permission to remain in rebellion.
The same God who repeatedly warned Pharaoh also provided a way of protection on the Passover night.
The same God who heard the cries of enslaved Israel later sent His Son into a world enslaved by sin.
And the same Jesus who offers forgiveness also calls us to follow Him.
Do not confuse patience with approval.
Do not mistake delayed consequences for divine indifference.
And do not assume that because God has been merciful to you, repentance can safely wait forever.
Pharaoh repeatedly delayed obedience.
And each refusal carried consequences that grew more terrible.
But you are reading this now.
You are breathing.
You are still able to turn toward Christ.
You do not have to repeat Pharaoh's response.
You can stop defending what God is calling you to surrender.
You can confess what you have been hiding.
You can seek forgiveness from the person you wounded.
You can turn away from a destructive pattern and ask God for the grace to walk differently.
You can come to Jesus without pretending that you have everything together.
Because Christianity is not the story of perfect people earning God's approval.
It is the story of a holy God redeeming sinners through His Son.
And if you have already trusted Christ, the story of Exodus still has something to say to you.
Do not become so accustomed to the language of grace that you forget the suffering of those around you.
The God who heard the enslaved Israelites calls His people to care about justice, mercy, and truth.
Do not use spiritual language to defend cruelty.
Do not use authority to crush those entrusted to your care.
Do not turn your home, workplace, ministry, or relationships into a smaller version of Pharaoh's palace.
Leadership is not ownership.
Power is not permission to oppress.
And obedience to God never requires us to abandon compassion.
If the story of Egypt teaches us anything, it is that the Lord takes seriously the cries of those who suffer.
And if the cross teaches us anything, it is that the Lord's mercy is greater than our ability to earn it.
Maybe that is why this account still disturbs us.
It refuses to let us reduce God to someone who exists merely to affirm our choices.
It refuses to let us pretend that evil is harmless.
It refuses to let us forget the victims of oppression.
And it refuses to let us believe that salvation is something we achieve through our own goodness.
It confronts the powerful.
It comforts the oppressed.
It warns the stubborn.
And it points the repentant toward mercy.
There is a reason the story does not end with Israel standing beside the Nile.
It moves toward deliverance.
Toward a journey through the wilderness.
Toward covenant.
Toward God's unfolding purpose of redemption.
And ultimately, through the whole witness of Scripture, toward Jesus Christ.
The greater Deliverer.
The true Passover Lamb.
The Savior who does not merely confront the bondage around us but addresses the sin within us.
And now I want to ask you something that may be more important than whether you agree with every theological detail in this article.
What part of this story exposed something in your own heart?
Was it Pharaoh's pride?
The suffering of innocent families?
God's patience?
The warning against delaying repentance?
Or the blood of the lamb, reminding you that your hope is not in your own righteousness but in God's mercy?
If Jesus has been restoring your life after a season of shame, failure, or wandering, share a little of what His grace has done.
Someone reading the comments may be struggling with the very thing Christ has already helped you begin to overcome.
Your testimony may remind them that repentance is not the end of hope.
It is the beginning of coming home.

And if you know someone who has been wrestling with the justice of God, someone wounded by abuse of power, or someone who thinks their past places them beyond forgiveness, consider sharing this article with them.
Because these conversations should not end when we finish reading.
They should lead us back to the Word of God.
They should lead us to prayer.
They should lead us to repentance, deeper faith, and greater love for Jesus Christ.
And if this ministry has helped you understand Scripture, rediscover hope, or draw nearer to the Savior, I want to invite you into something deeper.
Gospel Warrior is committed to helping people encounter the truth of God's Word, confront the reality of sin, and discover the transforming grace of Jesus Christ.
We want those resources to continue reaching people who are spiritually hungry, financially struggling, newly converted, wounded, searching, or simply longing to know the Lord more intimately.
But continuing and expanding this work requires faithful support.
Not because a payment makes someone more spiritual.
And certainly not because supporting one particular ministry is a biblical requirement for proving your love for Christ.
Salvation is free through the grace of God. Ministry support is a voluntary act of generosity.
Scripture encourages believers to support faithful Gospel work, but it also teaches that giving should never be forced or manipulated.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should come from a willing heart, not reluctantly or under compulsion.
If you regard that support as part of your personal Christian giving, do so prayerfully and in keeping with your biblical convictions and responsibilities to your local church.
Your prayers matter.
Your testimony matters.
Your willingness to share the Gospel matters.
These items are simply expressions of gratitude and opportunities to keep biblical encouragement close in everyday life. They are not the reason we preach Christ.
Jesus is the reason.
And if you have been looking for a meaningful way to support the ongoing creation and sharing of Gospel-centered resources, we would be grateful to have you walk alongside us.
We are not trying to build a community around merchandise.
We are not trying to sell forgiveness.
We are not trying to replace the local church.
We want to point people toward the crucified and risen Jesus Christ.
The One who saves sinners.
The One who calls the proud to repentance.
The One who draws near to the brokenhearted.
The One whose grace does not leave us unchanged.
And perhaps somewhere tonight, a person who has spent years hiding behind shame will finally understand that the Gospel is not a demand to become worthy before coming to Jesus.
It is an invitation to come to the only Savior who can make us new.
Perhaps a parent will read this and realize that authority should be exercised with humility rather than fear.
Perhaps a wounded believer will remember that God heard Israel's cries even before deliverance arrived.
Perhaps someone who has spent years resisting the Lord will finally stop making excuses.
Perhaps that someone is you.
The door to repentance is not closed simply because you have resisted God before.
Jesus still calls sinners to turn to Him.
And the promise of the Gospel is not that your past never happened.
It is that your past does not have to be the final word over your future.
Pharaoh had a throne, but his throne could not save him.
Egypt had riches, but its riches could not deliver it.
Israel had no earthly power sufficient to break its chains, but the Lord remembered His covenant.
And at Calvary, Jesus Christ accomplished the redemption that no human strength could ever achieve.
So when you remember the blood of Egypt's Passover, remember the Lamb of God.
When you remember Pharaoh's hardened heart, examine your own heart.
When you remember the cries of the oppressed, refuse to become indifferent to suffering.
And when you remember the terrible reality of judgment, do not forget the mercy offered through Jesus Christ.
Because the most important question is not whether you would have listened to Moses if you had lived in Egypt.
It is whether you will listen to the voice of Christ today.
If you are ready to turn toward Him, you can pray with honesty:

"Lord Jesus, I confess that I have sinned and that I cannot save myself. Forgive me. Have mercy on me. Teach me to surrender what I have been holding back. I believe You died for sinners and rose again. Help me trust You, follow You, and walk in the new life that only Your grace can give. Amen."
And when you finish praying, do not let this be another passing moment of emotion.
Open the Scriptures.
Read Exodus 7–12.
Read the Gospel of John.
Seek fellowship with a faithful local church.
Ask questions.
Keep learning.
And continue following Jesus.
Because the Lord who delivered His people from slavery is still worthy of our trust.
And the Savior who gave His life for sinners is still worthy of our surrender.
The greatest tragedy is not that Pharaoh lost his throne—it is that a heart can witness the power of God and still refuse the mercy of God.
